title: Clutch size
text:
3 Main Gaussian location-scale model
Data. The Bayesian model uses the same full dataset, with the age class from the existing binary age_class column.
The predictors operate at different hierarchical levels. Relative laying date is centred within season and is therefore identified primarily by comparisons among broods breeding in the same year; the model contains 12,627 brood records, with repeated observations of females accounted for by the female random intercept. Spring temperature and year vary only among seasons, so inference for these predictors is based on variation across 44 breeding seasons. Consequently, annual predictors are estimated from substantially fewer independent temporal units than within-season predictors.
Here rel_LD is laying date minus the annual median laying date, calculated in the validated reproductive dataset before the final clutch-model restrictions. Within-season centring separates variation in reproductive timing among females within a season from differences among seasons. It does not impose exact orthogonality in the final analytical sample: the observed individual-level correlations were 0.036 with spring temperature and 0.030 with year.
Model code.



Show model call

R/26_brms_clutch_main_no_tempsd_totoro.R

library(brms)
library(readr)
library(dplyr)

dat <- read_csv("data_derived/clutch_size_model_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(age_class = factor(age_class, levels = c("YOUNG", "OLD")),
         female_id = factor(female_id), year_f = factor(year_f))

priors_cs <- c(
  prior(normal(6, 2), class = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = "b"),
  prior(exponential(2), class = "sd"),
  prior(normal(-0.2, 0.5), class = "Intercept", dpar = "sigma"),
  prior(normal(0, 0.3), class = "b", dpar = "sigma"),
  prior(exponential(5), class = "sd", dpar = "sigma")
)

m_cs <- brm(
  bf(
    clutch ~ rel_LD + temp_mean_c + year_c + age_class +
      (1 | female_id) + (1 | year_f),
    sigma ~ rel_LD + temp_mean_c + year_c + age_class + (1 | year_f)
  ),
  family = gaussian(), prior = priors_cs, data = dat,
  backend = "cmdstanr", chains = 4, cores = 4,
  iter = 4000, warmup = 2000,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99, max_treedepth = 15),
  seed = 1981, init = 0, save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE)
)
saveRDS(m_cs, "models/brms/clutch_size_main_no_tempsd_full.rds")

Mean clutch size declined with relative laying date (\(\beta_{\mathrm{date}}^{(\mu)}\) = -0.0537, 95% CrI -0.0564 to -0.0509). 4.3 Clutch size and female age





Model-estimated mean clutch size (left) and residual inconsistency, expressed as sigma (right), for young and old females at the reference relative laying date, mean spring temperature, and mean study year. Points are predictions and error bars are 95% credible intervals; random effects are excluded.

Clutch size was higher among older than young females at the reference values of the continuous predictors. Broods produced by older females contained on average 0.181 more eggs (95% CrI 0.153 to 0.207). 4.4 Long-term temporal trends
We examined temporal change in clutch size and reproductive consistency after accounting for spring temperature.

Left: observed annual mean clutch size (grey points) and the population-level conditional temporal prediction. Right: conditional residual SD (sigma); higher values indicate lower reproductive consistency. Spring temperature is held at its study-wide mean, random effects are excluded, and ribbons show 95% credible intervals.

After accounting for spring temperature, mean clutch size showed a small positive temporal trend (\(\beta_{\mathrm{time}}^{(\mu)}\) = 0.0057, 95% CrI 0.0013 to 0.0100). The conditional predicted change from 1981 to 2025 was 0.253 eggs (95% CrI 0.056 to 0.442).
The temporal effect on residual scale was not clearly supported (\(\beta_{\mathrm{time}}^{(\sigma)}\) = 0.0021, 95% CrI -0.0014 to 0.0057). Across the study period, the conditional predicted change in \(\sigma\) was 9.6% (95% CrI -6.1 to 28.6%). This interval included zero; higher \(\sigma\) indicates lower reproductive consistency.

6 Robustness and inference limits
Alternative prior sets and the admissible log-Gaussian sensitivity fit retained the positive temperature association with mean clutch size and no clear temperature association with residual inconsistency. The age association with scale was distribution-dependent. The COM-Poisson fit yielded a non-positive-definite Hessian and unavailable likelihood-based fit statistics and was therefore excluded from inference. Individual-exposure extensions also failed admissibility checks. Scale effects describe variation among breeding attempts, not within-female repeatability.

title: Data and study population
text:
2 Relative laying date
Relative laying date is centred within breeding season using the annual median in the validated reproductive dataset:
\[
\mathrm{rel\_LD}_{iy}=\mathrm{LD}_{iy}-\mathrm{median}(\mathrm{LD}_{y}).
\]
For clutch size, relative date is inherited from the validated reproductive dataset before the final clutch-model restrictions. For fledging success only, it is re-centred after final sample restrictions, so its annual median is exactly zero. These are different centring stages and must not be described as identical. Model-specific checks of the annual mean, annual median, and association with window temperature are reported in the corresponding analysis chapters.

title: Overview
text:
Arct et al. 2026


Warmer springs are associated with larger clutches but lower egg-to-fledging success in a migratory passerine





0.1 Study aims


We asked how spring temperature was associated with reproductive performance in the collared flycatcher, and whether these responses were expressed through changes in average performance, reproductive consistency, or both.


Specifically, we examined:



whether mean spring temperature and residual interannual variability changed through time;


clutch size and its conditional consistency among breeding attempts were associated with spring temperature, relative laying date, female age, and long-term time;


fledging success and its conditional consistency among breeding attempts were associated with spring temperature, relative laying date, female age, and long-term time.



Current manuscript results. Mean temperature increased by 0.0439°C per year (95% CI [0.0248, 0.0630]). Warmer springs were associated with larger clutches and lower egg-to-fledging success. The reference model includes year random effects in both components and provides no clear evidence of a temperature association with fledging consistency. No clear temperature association with clutch-size inconsistency was detected. Scale effects describe heterogeneity among breeding attempts, not within-female repeatability.

An audit identified an indexing error in singlewin’s absolute weekly branch: the reference index used the month number plus 53 times the year offset, whereas climate records used the week number plus 52 times the year offset. The mean fledging-success association was negative for all four intervals. All precision intervals included zero under the new reference with year effects in both components. There was no clear temperature association with precision in any of the five tested intervals. The overlapping windows are correlated summaries of the same seasons, not independent replications. Precision describes extra-binomial heterogeneity at a given mean and clutch size, rather than raw outcome variance.
We therefore retain 26 March–7 May as the primary reproductive window; the alternatives are sensitivity checks, not candidates for post hoc selection.
The Bayesian clutch fits retain the original Gaussian model, including year-level random intercepts in both location and log residual SD. Female Gaussian random intercepts are integrated analytically with the exact marginal likelihood. The primary-window posterior is checked against the original brms output. Full convergence checks, computational-equivalence checks and coefficients scaled by the between-year temperature SD are retained in the sensitivity tables and local audit report.

title: Model structure
text: This chapter defines the three models used in the main analysis.

title: Model structure
text:
1 Temperature in the thermal window
For year \(t\),
\[
T_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_t,\sigma_t^2),
\]
\[
\mu_t=\beta_0^{(\mu)}+\beta_{\mathrm{time}}^{(\mu)}\mathrm{Time}_t,
\]
\[
\log(\sigma_t)=\gamma_0+\gamma_{\mathrm{time}}\mathrm{Time}_t.
\]
The Gaussian location–scale model uses 46 annual mean temperatures (1980–2025, including weather observations for 2020). Its location component estimates directional warming; its scale component estimates residual interannual SD around that trend. Higher environmental σ indicates lower interannual predictability in this operational sense. Time is centred on 2002.5. glmmTMB 1.1.14 uses log SD directly for Gaussian dispersion.

title: Model structure
text:
2 Clutch size
For brood \(r\),
\[
C_r \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_r,\sigma_r^2),
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mu_r={}&\beta_0^{(\mu)}+\beta_{\mathrm{LD}}^{(\mu)}\mathrm{relLD}_r+
\beta_T^{(\mu)}\bar T_r+\beta_{\mathrm{time}}^{(\mu)}\mathrm{Time}_r\\
&+\beta_{\mathrm{age}}^{(\mu)}\mathrm{Age}_r+u_{y[r]}+v_{f[r]},
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log(\sigma_r)={}&\beta_0^{(\sigma)}+
\beta_{\mathrm{LD}}^{(\sigma)}\mathrm{relLD}_r+
\beta_T^{(\sigma)}\bar T_r+\beta_{\mathrm{time}}^{(\sigma)}\mathrm{Time}_r\\
&+\beta_{\mathrm{age}}^{(\sigma)}\mathrm{Age}_r+w_{y[r]}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Higher \(\sigma\) indicates greater conditional residual dispersion among breeding attempts and therefore lower consistency.

title: Model structure
text:
3 Fledging success: reference specification
Here, fledging success is egg-to-fledging success: the number of fledglings relative to the number of eggs laid.
\[
K_r \sim \operatorname{BetaBinomial}(n_r,\mu_r,\phi_r),
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{logit}(\mu_r)={}&\beta_0^{(\mu)}+
\beta_{\mathrm{LD}}^{(\mu)}\mathrm{relLD}_r+
\beta_{\mathrm{age}}^{(\mu)}\mathrm{Age}_r+
\beta_{\mathrm{LD}\times\mathrm{age}}^{(\mu)}\mathrm{relLD}_r\mathrm{Age}_r\\
&+\beta_T^{(\mu)}\bar T_r+
\beta_{\mathrm{time}}^{(\mu)}\mathrm{Time}_r+u_{y[r]}+v_{f[r]},
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\log(\phi_r)=\beta_0^{(\phi)}+
\beta_{\mathrm{LD}}^{(\phi)}\mathrm{relLD}_r+
\beta_T^{(\phi)}\bar T_r+
\beta_{\mathrm{time}}^{(\phi)}\mathrm{Time}_r+
\beta_{\mathrm{age}}^{(\phi)}\mathrm{Age}_r+w_{y[r]}^{(\phi)}.
\]
Higher \(\phi\) means lower conditional extra-binomial overdispersion. This is residual heterogeneity conditional on the fitted predictors and random effects, not general phenotypic variance.

title: Model structure
text:
4 Notation
In the brood-level models, \(u_y\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau_{\mathrm{year}}^2)\) and \(v_f\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau_{\mathrm{female}}^2)\); \(w_y\) is the year-level scale effect in the clutch-size model. The predictor \(\bar T\) is mean temperature during 26 March–7 May, relLD is laying date centred within season, and Age is the binary class YOUNG/OLD.

title: Model structure
section: 5 Annual precision heterogeneity and zero-outcome sensitivity
text:
5 Annual precision heterogeneity and zero-outcome sensitivity
The reference includes independent year random intercepts in both location and log precision, and a female intercept in location. Temperature is common to broods within a year, so both components allow unexplained annual heterogeneity, paralleling the clutch-size model. For the fixed-precision LRT, the null retains the same random structure but uses only an intercept in the fixed precision component. A zero-augmented sensitivity fit adds a constant extra-zero probability, retaining those year effects. Its phi describes the beta-binomial component rather than the full mixture.

title: Model structure
text:
6 Reporting convention
Higher reproductive \(\sigma\) means greater inconsistency; higher \(\phi\) means greater consistency at a given mean success probability and clutch size. These are effects among breeding attempts, not repeatability of the same female. Coefficients are labelled \(\beta_j^{(\mu)}\), \(\beta_j^{(\sigma)}\) and \(\beta_j^{(\phi)}\). Clutch location is in eggs, fledging location on the logit scale, and scale effects on \(\log\sigma\) or \(\log\phi\). Temperature slopes are per °C, relative-date slopes per day and time slopes per year. Bayesian clutch estimates use 95% CrIs; frequentist temperature and fledging fits use 95% CIs. Simulation envelopes are neither CIs nor CrIs.

title: Fledging success
text:
The analysis includes 9,790 broods from 7,132 females in 39 seasons (1981–2019), including 2,315 complete failures (23.65%). The paired response is fledged and failed eggs, so the mean describes egg-to-fledging success, including complete failures.
Location contains relative laying date, age, their interaction, temperature and calendar year, with year and female random intercepts. Log precision contains relative date, age, temperature and calendar year, with a year random intercept. Annual temperature is shared by broods in the same year, and annual heterogeneity is allowed in both components, paralleling the clutch-size model. The two year effects are independent. Higher phi indicates lower extra-binomial heterogeneity at a given mean and clutch size; it describes breeding attempts, not within-female repeatability.

title: Fledging success
text:
4 Relative date and female age
Later breeding was associated with lower mean success and lower precision. The mean date–age interaction was −0.0181 (95% CI [−0.0328, −0.0035], p = 0.015). Location slopes were -0.0547 for yearlings and -0.0729 for older females, on the logit scale per day. The precision slope was −0.02235 per day (95% CI [−0.03091, −0.01380], p < 0.001). Date and age enter precision additively.
Older females had higher mean success at relative date zero (beta_age^(mu) = 0.1006, 95% CI [0.0256, 0.1755], p = 0.009) and higher precision (beta_age^(phi) = 0.1075, 95% CI [0.0151, 0.1999], p = 0.023). These contrasts were uncertain in the zero-augmented sensitivity fit.

title: Fledging success
text:
7 Complete-failure calibration and distributional sensitivity
The reference underestimated the observed 23.65% complete-failure fraction: fitted-mode simulations gave 20.07% (95% envelope [19.26, 20.84]); new-group simulations gave 19.21% [16.67, 22.15]. With approximate joint parameter uncertainty, the envelope widened to [15.89, 23.35]%, still below the observation at its upper limit. These checks omit conditional group-mode uncertainty and are not formal goodness-of-fit tests.
A zero-augmented sensitivity fit retained year effects in both components and reduced AIC by 740.78. Its precision-temperature coefficient was uncertain (−0.0854, CI [−0.2614, 0.0905]), while its conditional location coefficient remained negative (−0.2755, CI [−0.4184, −0.1325]). Approximate parameter uncertainty gave a zero-frequency envelope [19.92, 23.85]%. The mixing probability 0.1695 is not an identified biological fraction of failures; global coverage does not validate the full distribution.
